theory.intro: A sample is chosen from a population, and **how** it is chosen decides how far its result can be trusted. The four methods below differ in who gets a chance of being selected, and no sample size repairs an unfair method.
facts: **Simple random sample** — every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen from a list of the whole population.
**Systematic sample** — order the list, choose a random start, then take every $k$th member, where $k=\frac{\text{population size}}{\text{sample size}}$.
**Stratified sample** — divide the population into subgroups that matter for the question, then take from each subgroup in proportion to its share.
**Self-selected (voluntary-response) sample** — members decide for themselves whether to reply, so only those who chose to answer are counted.
Equal numbers from each subgroup are **not** a stratified sample: a subgroup holding a quarter of the population supplies a quarter of the sample.
Stratify by a variable **related to what is being measured**; splitting by an unrelated variable gains nothing.
A **larger sample** gives a more reliable estimate only when the method is fair.
A large self-selected sample simply repeats the same unfairness many more times.
Very small samples are unreliable because a few unusual members can swing the result.
A systematic sample fails when the list repeats a pattern that matches $k$, because then the same kind of member is chosen every time.
steps: Find the population total and the size of each subgroup
Divide each subgroup size by the population total
Multiply each fraction by the sample size
Check the subgroup samples add to the sample size

foundation.question_text: The Riverton Swim Club writes the name of each of its $400$ members on a slip, places every slip in a barrel, and draws out $40$ slips. Name the sampling method used.
foundation.solution_text:
Every member’s name is in the barrel, so every member has an equal chance of being drawn.
**Simple random sampling**.

foundation.question_text: A rail operator numbers the $600$ passengers who pass through a gate in the order they arrive, chooses a random start, then surveys every $20$th passenger from there. Name the sampling method used.
foundation.solution_text:
The passengers are put in an order and every $20$th one is taken after a random start.
**Systematic sampling**.

foundation.question_text: Kestrel University has four faculties of very different sizes. To survey $200$ students it selects students from each faculty in numbers proportional to that faculty’s share of all enrolments. Name the sampling method used.
foundation.solution_text:
The population is split into subgroups, and each subgroup supplies members in proportion to its size.
**Stratified sampling**.

foundation.question_text: Marlow Museum emails all $5000$ of its members a link to a survey, and reports the answers of the $380$ members who chose to reply. Name the sampling method used.
foundation.solution_text:
No member was selected by the museum; each member decided personally whether to reply.
**Self-selected (voluntary-response) sampling**.

foundation.question_text: A bank takes its alphabetical list of $10\,000$ customers, chooses a random start among the first $25$ names, then selects every $25$th name from there. Is this a simple random sample or a systematic sample? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
Only the starting name is random. Once it is fixed, every other selected customer is decided by the list order, so most groups of $400$ customers can never appear together.
In a simple random sample every possible group of $400$ customers is equally likely.
**It is a systematic sample**.

foundation.question_text: An airline has an ordered list of the $1500$ passengers who flew one route and wants a systematic sample of $60$ of them. Which passenger should be taken after the random start?
foundation.solution_text:
$k=\frac{1500}{60}$
$=25$
**Take every $25$th passenger on the list after the random start**.

foundation.question_text: A hardware chain takes a systematic sample from its ordered list of $900$ employees, using $k=45$ and starting at the $12$th name. Which are the first four employees selected?
foundation.solution_text:
Start at the $12$th name, then add $45$ each time.
$12+45=57$
$57+45=102$
$102+45=147$
**The $12$th, $57$th, $102$nd and $147$th employees**.

foundation.question_text:
A supermarket chain will take a stratified sample of $48$ of its $240$ store staff, using the departments below.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Department}&\textbf{Staff}\\ \hline \text{Bakery}&45\\ \text{Deli}&30\\ \text{Checkout}&90\\ \text{Stocking}&75\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&240\end{array}$
How many checkout staff should be in the sample?
foundation.solution_text:
Checkout staff make up $\frac{90}{240}$ of the staff.
$\frac{90}{240}\times 48$
$=\frac{3}{8}\times 48$
$=18$
**$18$ checkout staff**.

foundation.question_text: An insurance company asks $5$ of its $20\,000$ policyholders how they rate its claims service, and reports the result as the view of its policyholders. Explain why this result is unreliable.
foundation.solution_text:
With only $5$ responses, one unusually happy or unusually angry policyholder changes the reported figure by a fifth.
Five people cannot show the range of experiences across $20\,000$ policyholders.
**The sample is far too small for the result to be relied on**.

foundation.question_text: A paint manufacturer wants to check the amount of paint in the tins filled during a shift. The tins come off a moving line one after another. Which sampling method is the practical choice here, and why?
foundation.solution_text:
The tins arrive in an order and there is no list of them to draw names from before the shift ends.
Taking every $k$th tin as it passes needs no list and spreads the sample across the whole shift.
**Systematic sampling**.

foundation.question_text: A bus depot wants to know how its $140$ drivers rate the new rosters. It can either draw $20$ driver names at random from the staff list, or use the $20$ drivers who volunteer after a notice is put up. Which method gives the more reliable picture, and why?
foundation.solution_text:
Drawing names from the staff list gives every driver an equal chance of being selected, so drivers with every kind of view can appear.
Volunteers select themselves, so the $20$ who reply are the drivers who feel strongly enough about the rosters to come forward.
**Drawing $20$ names at random gives the more reliable picture**.

foundation.question_text: A state library service has $9000$ registered borrowers, each with a borrower number. Describe how it could take a simple random sample of $50$ borrowers.
foundation.solution_text:
Number the borrowers $1$ to $9000$ using the full register, so no borrower is left off the list.
Use a random number generator to produce $50$ different whole numbers from $1$ to $9000$.
**Survey the borrowers holding those $50$ numbers**.

development.question_text: A rail operator has an ordered list of the $2380$ passengers who travelled on one line in a morning and wants a systematic sample of $68$. Find the value of $k$, and explain why the starting passenger must be chosen at random.
development.solution_text:
$k=\frac{2380}{68}$
$=35$
So every $35$th passenger is taken.
If the start were always the first name, the same position in the list would be chosen every time the survey was run, and the earliest passengers of the morning would always be in the sample.
**Take every $35$th passenger, with the start chosen at random from the first $35$ names**.

development.question_text:
A state library service will survey $180$ of its $9000$ registered borrowers about opening hours, using a stratified sample by branch.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Branch}&\textbf{Borrowers}\\ \hline \text{Central}&4200\\ \text{Northgate}&1800\\ \text{Riverside}&1500\\ \text{Hillview}&900\\ \text{Seaton}&600\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&9000\end{array}$
How many borrowers should be taken from each branch?
development.solution_text:
$\frac{180}{9000}=\frac{1}{50}$, so each branch supplies $\frac{1}{50}$ of its borrowers.
Central: $\frac{4200}{50}=84$
Northgate: $\frac{1800}{50}=36$
Riverside: $\frac{1500}{50}=30$
Hillview: $\frac{900}{50}=18$
Seaton: $\frac{600}{50}=12$
$84+36+30+18+12=180$
**$84$, $36$, $30$, $18$ and $12$ borrowers**.

development.question_text:
Marlow Museum plans to survey $140$ of its $3500$ members by taking $35$ members from each of its four membership types.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{Membership type}&\textbf{Members}\\ \hline \text{Family}&900\\ \text{Adult}&1500\\ \text{Student}&400\\ \text{Senior}&700\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&3500\end{array}$
Explain why this plan is not a stratified sample, and give the numbers that would make it one.
development.solution_text:
A stratified sample takes from each subgroup in proportion to its size, but the four membership types are not the same size.
Under the plan the $400$ student members supply the same $35$ responses as the $1500$ adult members, so student members count more than four times as heavily as they should.
$\frac{140}{3500}=\frac{1}{25}$, so each type supplies $\frac{1}{25}$ of its members.
Family: $\frac{900}{25}=36$
Adult: $\frac{1500}{25}=60$
Student: $\frac{400}{25}=16$
Senior: $\frac{700}{25}=28$
**$36$ family, $60$ adult, $16$ student and $28$ senior members**.

development.question_text: An airline wants to know how its passengers rate the legroom on a long flight. It plans a stratified sample in which passengers are divided into subgroups by the first letter of their surname. Explain why this stratification gains nothing, and name a variable that would be a better basis for the strata.
development.solution_text:
Strata are only useful when the subgroups differ in what is being measured.
A passenger’s surname has nothing to do with the legroom they experienced, so each surname group would give much the same answer as any other.
**Stratify by cabin class instead**, because economy, premium and business seats have genuinely different legroom, and each class can then be represented in proportion to how many passengers it carried.

development.question_text: A bank shows a pop-up in its app asking customers to rate its service, and $12\,000$ of its $400\,000$ customers reply. A rival bank telephones $500$ customers chosen at random from its full customer list. Which bank has the more reliable estimate of how its customers rate its service? Justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
The first bank’s $12\,000$ replies all come from customers who chose to respond to a pop-up, so customers who ignore pop-ups are missing however many reply.
The rival’s $500$ customers were selected from the full list, so every customer had an equal chance of being contacted.
**The rival bank’s estimate is the more reliable**, because a fair method with $500$ responses beats an unfair one with $12\,000$.

development.question_text: A theatre wants to know how its patrons rate the seating. Patrons sit in the stalls, the circle or the balcony, and the three areas hold very different numbers of seats and give very different views of the stage. Which sampling method should the theatre use, and why?
development.solution_text:
The answer a patron gives depends heavily on which area they sat in, and the areas hold different numbers of patrons.
A method that guarantees each area is represented in proportion to its size is needed.
**Stratified sampling, with the stalls, circle and balcony as the strata**, each supplying a share of the sample equal to its share of the seats sold.

development.question_text: The Riverton Swim Club wants to know how its $400$ members rate the new pool timetable. It can either draw $60$ names at random from the membership list, or post the survey on the club’s social-media page and use the replies. Compare the two methods and state which result the committee should act on.
development.solution_text:
Drawing $60$ names from the membership list gives every member an equal chance of selection, including members who never look at social media.
Posting the survey lets members choose themselves, so the replies come from members who follow the page and felt like answering — probably those most annoyed or most pleased with the timetable.
**The committee should act on the $60$ names drawn at random**, because only that method reaches members of every kind.

development.question_text: A paint manufacturer fills $2000$ tins during a shift and wants a systematic sample of $40$ of them for testing. Describe in full how the sample should be taken.
development.solution_text:
$k=\frac{2000}{40}$
$=50$
Choose a random whole number from $1$ to $50$ as the starting tin — say the $23$rd tin off the line.
Then take every $50$th tin after it: the $73$rd, the $123$rd, the $173$rd, and so on.
**Continue until $40$ tins have been taken, which covers the whole shift evenly**.

development.question_text: A hardware chain surveys $6$ of its $900$ employees, chosen at random, and reports that its staff are satisfied with the new rosters. Explain the weakness in this study, and state what would improve it.
development.solution_text:
The method is fair, because the $6$ were chosen at random, but $6$ responses cannot show the range of views across $900$ employees.
If two of the six happen to work in the one store with a good roster, the reported result swings sharply.
**Survey many more employees, still chosen at random from the full staff list**, so that unusual individuals no longer dominate the result.

development.question_text: The Riverton Swim Club sorts its $400$ members by membership number, picks a random start between $1$ and $10$, then takes every $10$th member from there. The secretary records this as a stratified sample of $40$. Name the method actually used, and explain the difference.
development.solution_text:
Taking every $10$th name from an ordered list after a random start is **systematic sampling**.
A stratified sample would first split the members into subgroups that matter for the question — age groups, or squad levels — and then take from each subgroup in proportion to its size.
**The club’s method uses the list order only and never divides the members into subgroups at all**.

mastery.question_text:
An insurance company will survey $200$ of its $20\,000$ policyholders about its claims service, and wants to compare the ratings given in each state.
$\begin{array}{lc}\textbf{State}&\textbf{Policyholders}\\ \hline \text{NSW}&8000\\ \text{Vic}&6000\\ \text{Qld}&4000\\ \text{SA}&1500\\ \text{Tas}&500\\ \hline \textbf{Total}&20\,000\end{array}$
Give the numbers a stratified sample by state would take, and justify why stratifying by state suits this aim better than a simple random sample of $200$ drawn from the combined list.
mastery.solution_text:
$\frac{200}{20\,000}=\frac{1}{100}$, so each state supplies $\frac{1}{100}$ of its policyholders.
NSW: $\frac{8000}{100}=80$
Vic: $\frac{6000}{100}=60$
Qld: $\frac{4000}{100}=40$
SA: $\frac{1500}{100}=15$
Tas: $\frac{500}{100}=5$
$80+60+40+15+5=200$
Stratifying fixes those numbers in advance, so every state contributes and each state’s share of the sample matches its share of the policyholders.
A simple random sample of $200$ from the combined list is fair, but the number drawn from each state is left to chance, and Tasmania — with $\frac{1}{40}$ of the policyholders — could easily supply only one or two responses, or none at all.
**Take $80$, $60$, $40$, $15$ and $5$ policyholders; stratifying guarantees each state is represented in proportion, which is exactly what a state-by-state comparison needs**.

mastery.question_text: An airline emailed a satisfaction survey to all $900\,000$ passengers who flew with it last year, and $20\,000$ replied. Its report says the result is reliable because $20\,000$ is a very large sample. A rival airline telephoned $600$ passengers chosen at random from its full passenger list. Each airline is estimating satisfaction among its own passengers. Explain which of the two figures is the more reliable estimate, and why the far larger number of responses does not settle the question.
mastery.solution_text:
The $20\,000$ replies were not selected by the airline — each of those passengers chose to answer, so the group is made up of passengers who felt strongly enough to open the email and complete the survey.
The $880\,000$ passengers who did not reply are not represented at all, and nothing in the data shows how their ratings would compare.
The rival’s $600$ passengers were drawn from the full passenger list, so every passenger had an equal chance of being contacted, including those who would never answer an email.
Sample size and sampling method do different jobs: a larger sample reduces how much a fair estimate swings by chance, but it does nothing about a method that leaves out most of the population. Emailing $9$ million passengers and taking whoever replies would still describe only the passengers who reply.
**The rival airline’s $600$ telephoned passengers give the more reliable estimate**.

mastery.question_text: A supermarket chain keeps its staff list ordered store by store. Within each store the manager is listed first, followed by that store’s $11$ other staff, so each store occupies $12$ consecutive entries. The chain takes a systematic sample by starting at the $1$st name and then taking every $12$th name. Explain why this sample gives a badly distorted result, and state one change that fixes it.
mastery.solution_text:
Starting at name $1$ and stepping by $12$ selects names $1$, $13$, $25$, $37$, and so on.
Each store occupies $12$ entries with the manager first, so every one of those positions is a manager.
The step size $k=12$ matches the repeating pattern in the list exactly, so the sample contains managers only and no other staff member can ever be selected. A survey of pay or workload would then report managers’ conditions as though they were the whole chain’s.
**Break the match between $k$ and the pattern** — for example, sort the whole staff list by employee number rather than store by store before sampling, or choose a step size that is not a multiple of $12$, such as every $13$th name.
